title: Holi: the festival of colors
hookLine: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
carry: the name of god outlasts the fire
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
last: FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.

lines: A STRANGER SMEARS PINK ON YOUR CHEEK.
NOBODY CAN TELL WHO IS WHO.
cards: A street in north India, on a spring morning. Somebody's uncle is purple. A grandmother is laughing with green powder in her hair.
A stranger you've never met walks up, says happy Holi, and smears pink on your cheek, and you do the same back. Water balloons from a balcony. Drums from somewhere.
By noon you can't tell the banker from the delivery driver, or the neighbor you haven't spoken to in a year from your own cousin. Everyone is the same muddy, glorious color.
But the night before, there was a fire, and the fire is where the story is.

teach.h: A BOY WHO KEEPS SAYING THE NAME.
teach.b: The story is about a boy named Prahlad. His father, Hiranyakashipu, is a demon king with a boon that makes him nearly impossible to kill, and he decides that makes him God. Everyone in the kingdom must worship him.
His own son won't. Prahlad keeps saying the name of Vishnu. The Bhagavata Purana tells how his father tries everything: snakes, elephants, a cliff, poison.
The boy survives each one. Then comes the part the festival remembers.
The king's sister, Holika, is said to be protected from fire. She takes Prahlad on her lap and sits down in a blazing pyre. And the fire turns.

Holika burns. The boy walks out unharmed, still saying the name. An honest note: the Bhagavata tells Prahlad's story and ends it with Narasimha; the Holika scene comes from later tellings and the festival itself.
Either way, the heart is the same, and it's one of Hinduism's most loved practices: the Name.
Repeating God's name, called japa, or singing it together, kirtan. Prahlad had no army, only the name, and in the story it was enough.
So on the full-moon night of Phalguna, at the end of winter, people light bonfires called Holika Dahan, and many walk around them, remembering a fire that couldn't hold a child.

teach.h: THE NAME OF GOD OUTLASTS THE FIRE.
teach.b: The next morning, the colors. People say it with a grin: bura na mano, Holi hai. Don't be offended, it's Holi.
For one day the lines between people get smudged on purpose, and old quarrels are supposed to end. Holi has other stories too, and i'll come back for them.

how: Hindus light the Holika Dahan bonfire on the full-moon night of Phalguna and, the next morning, throw colored powder and water with family, neighbors and strangers alike; many use the day to make up after quarrels.

a day of fasting for Vishnu

the Bhagavata tells Prahlad's story and Narasimha; the Holika scene comes from later tellings and the festival.
Holi begins the night before, with a bonfire
Holika Dahan: bonfires on the full-moon night of Phalguna.
on Holi, only family throws color at each other

games.q: you're Prahlad. your father is king, and he orders everyone, you included, to worship him. what do you do?
o: worship him, and keep Vishnu secretly in your heart.
keep saying Vishnu's name, out loud.
games.why: he keeps saying the name, through snakes, poison and fire. in the festival's story, he walks out of Holika's fire unharmed.

practice: Choose a name of God: Hari, Rama, Krishna, Shiva, or simply Ma. Say it slowly, eleven times, out loud or inside, counting on your fingers, the way Prahlad kept saying his. Think of a place where saying what you believe feels hard.
If you don't pray, choose one word that holds what you stand for. Then picture tomorrow's colors, and one person you'd smudge first, to make up.

wordCard.voice: Holi. The spring festival of colors, the morning after the bonfire that remembers Prahlad walking out of the fire.

orig.note: Hindi: the festival's name, often linked to Holika, whose bonfire the night before begins it.

carryVoice: Your line: the name of god outlasts the fire. Prahlad had only the name, and it was enough. That's day eighty-two.
